blocks.text: Oseas XIII, 3., to show how vain is the glory of those who think themselves safe under the protection of the idols they worship. They shall be, he says, as the morning cloud, [col. 480] and as the dew that passes away early, as the chaff that is driven by the whirlwind out of the threshing floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.] The chimney there is ארבה arubba, for which the Greeks read ארבה arbe, that is, locust; for these two words, though they differ greatly in their vowel points, nevertheless have the same letters. Hence arose the Greek version ὡς ἀτμὶς ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων [hōs atmis apo akridōn], as vapour from locusts. And a most learned and most pious man understands a mist consisting of locusts, which obscures the light of the sun but, passing quickly, soon vanishes and restores the sunlight that it had, as it were, intercepted for a short time. Jerome understands the very breath of the locusts, saying that Ephraim is compared to ἀτμῷ [atmō], that is, to vapour, or to the breath and air which comes out of the mouth of the locust so thinly that it is not perceived. Theodoret says that the wicked are to be destroyed just as ἀτμὸν, ἐν ἀέρι γινόμενον, νέφος ἀκρίδων ἐπιγινόμενον διαλύει [atmon, en aeri ginomenon, nephos akridōn epiginomenon dialyei], a cloud [III, 316] of locusts, falling upon it, dissolves a vapour raised in the air. But what the Greeks thought matters little, since the Hebrew text has something else, namely smoke from the chimney, ἀπὸ καπνοδόχης [apo kapnodochēs], as Theodotion rightly rendered it. And Cyril follows this. Seneca too uses the comparison of smoke and cloud on a similar theme, Troades, Act 2.
— — as dark smoke from hot fires vanishes within a brief space; as the onset of Arctic Boreas scatters the heavy clouds we saw just now: so this spirit by which we are ruled flows away.

Verse 11. And the Lord uttered his voice before his army, that his camp may be very great, that he may be strong who executes his word. For the day of the Lord is great and very terrible: and who can abide it?] That is, "The Lord by his word has enlisted great forces, to execute upon sinners a heavy judgment which no one can withstand." This seems to be the Prophet's meaning, although the interpreters think very differently. And here the threats end. They are followed by exhortations to repentance and by many promises in God's name. Among these, since they concern the locusts, we shall also explain what is found in the twentieth and twenty-fifth verses.
